title: How to Know When It’s Time to Reinvent Yourself | Tiger Sisters Live
guest: Ally Maki (actress, founder/CEO of Asian American Girl Club) and Jenna Ushkowitz (Glee actress, Broadway producer, COO of Asian American Girl Club)
summary: The first-ever Tiger Sisters live show, with audience Q&A on shedding the grind mentality, marketing yourself, negotiating, and adult friendships, followed by a conversation with Ally Maki and Jenna Ushkowitz of Asian American Girl Club on how to know when it is time to reinvent yourself. Main takeaways: boredom and 'exciting scared' signal it is time to move, most reinventions come from rock bottom rather than glamour, putting yourself out there creates unexpected collisions, and community and practice make the scary asks easier.

ideas.idea: What got you here will not get you to the next step, and the teeth-gritted grind mentality of your 20s is not sustainable into your 30s.
ideas.detail: Cherie says grinding late nights got them their careers but burns you out; there is no honor in grinding just to grind, and she is shedding that belief for the new decade.

ideas.idea: No situation in your life is permanent unless you want it to be, whether you are in a great place or an unhappy one.
ideas.detail: Jean says she barely recognizes her own life two years into Tiger Sisters after leaving corporate; things change all the time.

ideas.idea: Sustainability, not balance, is the goal: weave friendships, hobbies and your life into the work so the second year does not burn you out like the first.
ideas.detail: Jean keeps many hobbies (pottery, swimming, tennis) and says the first year of building Tiger Sisters felt really tough because of the workload.

ideas.idea: Investing in your whole self, including appearance, is healthier than believing your only value is your brain, a message Asian women rarely hear.
ideas.detail: Cherie learned hair, took a makeup class with Kelly Zhang and got her colors done in the last year and wishes she had done it earlier instead of focusing only on being smart and hardworking.

ideas.idea: No one will tell your story or care about your career more than you, so marketing yourself is a job: decide the values and features you want to be known for when you enter a room.
ideas.detail: Cherie posts daily on Instagram and LinkedIn; Jean adds two mindsets learned from her: treat personal branding as a fun, lighthearted project, and remember times someone else's content genuinely helped you, so sharing is helping people.

ideas.idea: Having a co-founder or co-pilot makes putting yourself out there and building anything easier because you can bounce ideas off each other.
ideas.detail: Jean, a very private person, made a complete career pivot into media and credits having her sister as a partner; Cherie notes Jean's transformation over two years shows anyone can do it.

ideas.idea: A clear mission grounds you against the fear of looking cringey: if everything is in service of the goal, who cares what people think.
ideas.detail: The Tiger Sisters mission is to empower and uplift a billion women; they were once too bashful to say it out loud but now state it openly because it anchors every decision.

ideas.idea: If you don't ask, nothing changes; if you do, something great can happen, so treat negotiation as 'what's the best that can happen' even if you hate confrontation.
ideas.detail: Cherie dislikes confrontation but has learned to run toward the fire, since no one cares more about your career than you.

ideas.idea: The biggest negotiation tip is that you never have to respond in the moment: keep a poker face, say 'great information, let me take it back,' and set a follow-up meeting.
ideas.detail: Practice out loud in the mirror or with a friend for 10 minutes; hearing yourself say it once does something to the neurons, and business school even had a class on role-playing tough conversations like raises and promotions.

ideas.idea: Adult friendships need intentional, recurring structure, like an annual retreat with a fixed group.
ideas.detail: Jean and about 20 women from her HBS class meet for one weekend every year, sometimes with programming like a fireside chat with a classmate who is CFO of a public company.

ideas.idea: Friendship is all about follow-up, and it takes two; it is fine for friendships and your social life to fade in and out across seasons.
ideas.detail: Cherie says a friend may be in a busy season with work or a new partner, and it is okay to be very social for a quarter or a year and then less so.

ideas.idea: Success is not grinding alone; it comes from bouncing ideas off other people and from friendship.
ideas.detail: Jean points out Cherie is working today with her best friend from college.

ideas.idea: Boredom is a good sign it is time to change, and there are two kinds of scared: the 'something is wrong, get out' fear and the exciting, challenging scared that signals the next chapter.
ideas.detail: Ally Maki says she listens to those feelings to guide her path; Jenna says when faced with two paths she picks the scarier one, meaning the one she has never done before.

ideas.idea: Reinvention requires letting go of seeing yourself as one trait or path.
ideas.detail: Jenna told her partner 'I'm just a comedy person' and it took a long time to accept she could do drama or start something like AAGC.

ideas.idea: Careers that look glamorous from outside are often driven by rock-bottom moments: after Glee, none of the cast could get hired because nobody could see them as anything but their characters.
ideas.detail: Jenna pivoted to producing and back to Broadway, which was terrifying because everyone was watching what she would do next; Ally says the biggest parts of her journey came from rock bottom, including becoming a multi-hyphenate out of need.

ideas.idea: Career paths zigzag and you can only connect the dots looking backward; during the lull or pivot it is terrifying.
ideas.detail: The hosts note that Instagram and LinkedIn show only the shiny exterior, not the lulls in between.

ideas.idea: A 'failure' with 70 views is still 70 real people, and you never know who is in the room: Ally's self-made YouTube video with her dog got her cast in Toy Story without an audition.
ideas.detail: Pixar's casting department found the video on YouTube and said 'that's the character'; the hosts tie it to the Lady Gaga line that in a room of 100 people you only need one to believe in you.

ideas.idea: Putting yourself out there, whether content or events, opens room for collisions and opportunities you cannot predict.
ideas.detail: Hosts' takeaway from Ally's story: be brave.

ideas.idea: Founder imposter syndrome persists even after success when you started something by accident out of a need.
ideas.detail: Ally started AAGC by asking 'does anyone else feel this way' and people came from everywhere; she still thinks of herself as 'just an actor' and is learning to step into 'I am a founder'.

ideas.idea: Loving the people you work with is life's true luxury; the ups and downs of building something are much less lonely with a partner.
ideas.detail: Jenna joined Ally at AAGC after having her second child, having admired the community Ally bootstrapped for seven years; they are now CEO and COO on Zoom for hours daily, and once competed for the same roles as 'phantom' rivals.

ideas.idea: The persistent challenge for Asian American women is asking for more; the post-ask embarrassment fades with practice and no one can take your story or perspective from you.
ideas.detail: Ally used to feel she sounded unhumble after standing up for herself in press interviews, but pushing through gets easier every time; Jenna adds that people ask because they want to hear from you, so speaking up matters.

ideas.idea: Beautiful things come from moments of discomfort, and the second half of running toward the hard thing is knowing people will support you on the other side.
ideas.detail: AAGC would not exist without people who wore the shirt or talked about it in rooms; teaming up is a morale booster because 'this is hard, but at least we're in this together'.

ideas.idea: Community is real life: look at the person next to you, put your ask on the board, and both offer and receive help.
ideas.detail: The live show included a reciprocity ring and whiteboard for asks, from recommendations to babysitters to travel tips.

ideas.idea: Reinvention is not becoming a different person but becoming more yourself.
ideas.detail: Closing line of the live show, addressed to a room of people trying to become, return to, or rediscover something.

ideas.idea: Audience survey results: the top dating red flag is having no friends, people overspend most on eating out and DoorDash, and AI is the number one thing people pretend to understand.
ideas.detail: From the Tiger Family Feud segment polling about 150 attendees; 'we're like a family' was voted the worst corporate phrase and girls trips tied with new hobbies as the best heartbreak cure.
